extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of political theory / history of ideas
extracted.subtask_description: A political-philosophical essay arguing how ‘government by discussion’ (deliberative, parliamentary institutions and customary law) produces social benefits: checking hasty action, fostering intellectual life and originality, creating cooperative groups, and enabling verifiable progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polity of discussion as a brake on hasty action
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If you want to stop instant and immediate action, always make it a condition that the action shall not begin till a considerable number of persons have talked over it, and have agreed on it.' Government by discussion prevents excessive rapidity and ensures elaborate consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: multiple temperaments/ideas produce spokesmen, objections and counter-proposals so 'in the end nothing will probably be done, or at least only the minimum which is plainly urgent.' Exception: where rapid, centralized command is required (e.g., military campaigns), deliberation may be harmful. Anti-pattern: praising 'an age of committees' as inherently useless ignores the deliberative check's benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative government cultivates an intellectual tone and habit of weighing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A government requiring constant debates (written and oral) fosters 'a diffused disposition to weigh evidence, a conviction that much may be said on every side of everything.' This diminishes inherited 'barbaric impulse' and bigotry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects: increases doubt, reduces persecution based on unexamined dogma, and spreads skeptical, evidence-oriented habits through society. Examples: debates and written discussion as causes of broader intellectual caution. Anti-pattern: treating such caution as a mere lack of energy or vigor—author argues it is a civilising benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polity of discussion promotes originality and inventive activity
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Nothing promotes intellect like intellectual discussion, and nothing promotes intellectual discussion so much as government by discussion.' The essay argues that deliberative institutions quicken and enliven thought across society, leading to inventions and originality (e.g., English artisans generating useful suggestions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence/Examples: Locke/Newton/Darwin cited as instances; artisans in England described as 'more inventive than any other artisan.' Guidance: valuing the spread of intellectual atmosphere as a source of progress and economic/technical innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government by discussion fosters 'animated moderation'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Animated moderation'—a union of spirit and measure—is a quality produced by discussion-based polity: energetic yet restrained action, vigorous judgment without excess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character: writings and actions that are 'never slow, are never excessive, are never exaggerated;' practical examples include Scott, Homer, Shakespeare (partly), and statesmen like Lord Palmerston who 'went with a great swing' but 'never tumbled over.' Institutional effect: weeds out idiosyncratic extreme minds; produces vigour with moderation suited to active life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay and deliberation have trade-offs (need for decisiveness in some contexts)
rubrics_metrics.description: While deliberation prevents hasty action, in many cases quick action will be preferable; 'A campaign ... cannot be directed by a debating society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: recognize contexts requiring centralized rapid decision-making versus those benefitting from deliberation. The rubric implies evaluators must balance speed and deliberation depending on domain (e.g., military vs. legislative policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiable progress defined as increased adaptation to environment
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Verifiable progress' (the sort most people will admit) is characterised by: (1) greater command over the powers of nature, (2) improved internal organization of people as 'machines' (self-regulation), and (3) better knowledge of how to use powers for present health and comfort—summed as an increase of adaptation of man to his environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational test: prefer measures that most people accept (material comfort, control over nature, capacity to foresee and provide for future). Excludes highly disputed moral/religious changes. Use these concrete indicators to judge progress rather than contested aesthetic or moral claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress requires cooperative groups and felt union (similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The progress of MAN requires the co--operation of MEN ... The first principle ... is that man can only progress in 'co-operative groups' ... the members of such a group should be similar enough to one another to co-operate easily and readily together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: imitation of admired character-types multiplies them; social cohesion depends on 'felt union' of heart and spirit. Institutional implication: stable customs, family structures, and shared beliefs create the likeness necessary for effective cooperation. Anti-pattern: assuming isolated individual advances suffice for broad social progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of customary law and isolation in forming cooperating characters
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This needful co-operation and this requisite likeness ... I believe to have been produced by ... the authority of 'customary law.' ... In its earlier stage this is ... a stern, incessant, implacable rule.' Customary law and social isolation create the character-models that make cooperative society possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/Examples: early societies benefit from privacy and secrecy while forming cohesive customs (Greece, Rome, Judaea). Trade and foreign intercourse can be disruptive in these formative stages. Anti-pattern: romanticising liberty in contexts where fixed custom was the practical force that produced social cohesion and subsequent progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions that confer competitive (military/social) advantage tend to spread civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Better institutions (e.g., compact family systems, stronger religions that give 'confidence in the universe') have a physical/military advantage over worse ones, leading to their spread and the conquest of less organized peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: societies with patrilineal/compact family systems are argued to be better bases for military discipline and hence have 'possessed the earth.' Guidance: when assessing institutional quality, include their capacity to produce social cohesion and competitive advantage, not only abstract moral claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress paradox: individual incentives exist but collective progress remains rare
rubrics_metrics.description: Although individual inventors receive rewards and 'nature gives a prize to every single step,' verifiable progress is historically rare; the essay treats this as a puzzle requiring institutional explanation (cooperation, customs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for evaluation: when judging causes of (lack of) progress, consider systemic/institutional barriers (e.g., absence of cooperative groups) rather than solely individual incentives; look for second-order effects (modeling of character) that amplify or block progress.
